14.0.0.en: 1 O Israel, return unto the LORD thy God; for thou hast fallen by thine iniquity. 2 Take with you words, and turn to the LORD: say unto him, Take away all iniquity, and receive us graciously: so will we render the calves of our lips. 3 Asshur shall not save us; we will not ride upon horses: neither will we say any more to the work of our hands, Ye are our gods: for in thee the fatherless findeth mercy.

14.0.1.en: The final call came: "Return, O Israel, unto the LORD thy God; for thou hast stumbled by thine iniquity. Take with you words, and turn to the LORD" [1-2]. So our heavenly Bridegroom keeps calling us all the days of our exile, until our last breath, urging us to return to Him. He does not compel us to return by force, but entreats us with His love and draws our heart by His continual calling and declarations. As Abba Mark the Ascetic says: [No power can force us to do good or evil; rather, the one to whom we freely yield our will, whether God or Satan, urges us on to the work that belongs to his kingdom.]

14.0.2.en: He calls us and keeps on calling us, but He does not compel us, for He esteems our human freedom and deals with us on the level of mutual love, not as lifeless machines in His hands. As St. John Chrysostom says: [We are masters, able to make every member in us an instrument of evil or an instrument of righteousness (in Christ Jesus).] Just as man commits iniquity with full freedom, so it is fitting that he return to the Lord his God with full freedom, asking for divine help to support him in returning.

14.0.3.en: The first step on the way of repentance is the awareness of error, for He says: "for thou hast stumbled (fallen) by thine iniquity." Therefore it is fitting for you to return to the Lord your God bearing with you "words," which are your confession of the error. For whoever perceives in the depths of his heart that he has fallen because of his iniquity is not at a loss for words, nor does he ask: What shall I confess? Or how shall I confess? For the Holy Spirit, who exposes his iniquities to him, is the One who supports him in confessing them.

14.0.4.en: Here we want to affirm that confession is not merely a listing of the sins or iniquities we have committed, but first and before everything else it is a feeling of bitterness over what we have done. As Abba Mark the Ascetic says: [The experienced man who learns the truth confesses his sins to God, not by counting up what he has done but by the bitterness of his soul over what he suffers.] And as Fr. John of Kronstadt says: [Let us hasten to entreat God with repentance and tears. Let us enter into ourselves and contemplate our unclean hearts with all exactness, for when we see the multitudes of abominations that hinder the grace of God, we perceive that we are spiritually dead.]

14.1.0.en: This confession has two complementary aspects: acknowledging the error, and faith in God, the Giver of goodness. As St. Augustine says, we confess our sins to God just as we confess His work in us, praising Him. "Say unto him, Take away all iniquity, and receive us graciously (what is good): so will we render the calves of our lips" [2]. We ask Him to take away from us every iniquity we have committed, and to grant us everything good that comes from Him, which we have lost; the sacrifices of thanksgiving are "the calves of our lips," or the fruit of our lips, according to the Septuagint.

14.2.0.en: We have perceived the iniquity that killed our heart and put our inner soul to death, and we have confessed God as the Giver of the virtuous life that comes from Him and binds us to Him as the only Savior. So we do not lean on the arm of a man, whatever that arm may be, saying: "Asshur shall not save us; we will not ride upon horses: neither will we say any more to the work of our hands, Ye are our gods." For the people of Israel at that time, this meant realizing that Asshur, on whom they had leaned, did not save them but crushed them and took them captive; that their military power, "the horses," could not rescue them from God's wrath against them because of their wickedness; and that the idols of Baal, which were the work of their hands, were not in truth their gods able to support them. This is one aspect; on the other hand, God wished to declare the separation of the political side from the spiritual side. Salvation is not accomplished by a human arm, however great its might, authority or greatness, like Asshur, nor by temporal power like the horses, nor by gods that are made by our own hands... Rather, salvation is from God. In other words, may we not lean on Asshur, that is, on others, nor on our own power, gifts and personal abilities (the horses), nor on our own righteousness (our inner gods), but say: "in thee the fatherless findeth mercy" [3]. Without You I have become an orphan with no heavenly Father, so who will have mercy on me but You?! As St. Jerome says: [The fatherless are those who have lost God their Father.]

14.3.0.en: 4 I will heal their backsliding, I will love them freely: for mine anger is turned away from him. 5 I will be as the dew unto Israel: he shall grow as the lily, and cast forth his roots as Lebanon. 6 His branches shall spread, and his beauty shall be as the olive tree, and his smell as Lebanon. 7 They that dwell under his shadow shall return; they shall revive as the corn, and grow as the vine: the remembrance thereof shall be as the wine of Lebanon. 8 Ephraim shall say, What have I to do any more with idols? I have heard him, and observed him: I am like a green fir tree. From me is thy fruit found. 9 Who is wise, and he shall understand these things? prudent, and he shall know them? for the ways of the LORD are right, and the just shall walk in them: but the hypocrites shall fall therein.

14.3.1.en: If Israel has come into a diseased condition that is hard, indeed impossible, to cure, then God is the only Physician able to heal him, for He says: "I will heal their backsliding" [4].

14.3.2.en: And as St. Paphnutius says: [In truth, the saints never say that they have reached that way in which they walk, with progress and perfection in virtue, by their own striving, but by the grace of God, saying: "Lead me in thy truth" (Ps 25:5).]

14.3.3.en: The Lord comes forward as a true Physician who heals the backsliding soul, and His motive for this work is pure, free love. "I will heal their backsliding, I will love them freely (without cost): for mine anger is turned away from him" [4]. The Physician has declared His healing love, saying: "For God so loved the world, that he gave his only begotten Son, that whosoever believeth in him should not perish, but have everlasting life" (Jn 3:16).

14.3.4.en: What has the Physician offered to His beloved patients?

14.3.5.en: "I will be as the dew unto Israel: he shall grow as the lily, and cast forth his roots as Lebanon.

14.3.6.en: His branches (his boughs) shall spread, and his beauty shall be as the olive tree, and his smell as Lebanon.

14.3.7.en: They that dwell under his shadow shall return; they shall revive as the corn, and grow as the vine (the grapevine).

14.3.8.en: The remembrance thereof shall be as the wine of Lebanon.

14.4.0.en: Ephraim shall say, What have I to do any more with idols?" [5-8].

14.4.1.en: In brief, we can say that God offers them Himself as dew coming down from heaven to water them; He refreshes them and makes them like the blooming lily; He renews them inwardly so that their hidden roots go deep; He makes them grow spiritually so that their branches spread without ceasing; He grants them spiritual beauty and glory so that they are like the olive tree in its splendor; He pours out His fragrance upon them so that they have the smell of Lebanon; He uses them for the rest of many, so that many gather under their shadows, and for the joy of many, as they blossom like the vine; and their good remembrance is never cut off.

14.4.2.en: First: "I will be as the dew unto Israel" [5]. Long ago the Lord said to Moses: "Behold, I will rain bread from heaven for you" (Ex 16:4), and it was said: "And when the dew fell upon the camp in the night, the manna fell upon it" (Num 11:9). But now He does not send bread down to us; rather, He Himself came down to us, offering His holy Body as heavenly bread that satisfies the heart. He came down to us as dew that quenches the flame of the passions, descending upon our inner camp to make it His own camp and dwelling. He comes down by night, in the midst of our darkness, in secret, to turn it into bright day.

14.4.3.en: When the three youths were cast into the furnace of fire, the Word of God appeared with them, and the furnace became dew for them; likewise, if the world becomes a fire and a furnace, the Lord Christ appears in us and turns our life into dew!

14.4.4.en: Second: "He shall grow as the lily." The heavenly Bridegroom says: "I am the rose of Sharon, and the lily of the valleys" (Song 2:1), and here He makes His people a blooming lily. As Origen says: [He became the lily of the valleys only so that His beloved too might become a lily, imitating Him... that is, every soul that draws near to Him, follows His steps and imitates Him becomes a lily.] St. Gregory, Bishop of Nyssa, sees that the soul, like the lily, rises straight upward toward the Messiah, its true Vinedresser. He lifts it above the cares of this life and the thorns of sin that choke the soul (Mk 4:18), and raises it above the dust of this life so that it is not defiled. Thus the Lord Christ refreshes His Church, granting her "all spiritual blessings in heavenly places" (Eph 1:3), so that she bears His heavenly traits and fulfills His mission in her.

14.4.5.en: Third: "and cast forth his roots as Lebanon." If the Church, by clinging to the Lord Christ, comes to bear His uprightness and the fellowship of His nature, and so is counted like Him a lily in the wilderness among the thorns, then the secret of this life is her hidden roots, or her roots that enjoy the work of His grace, so that she bears His life in her and says with the Apostle Paul: "By the grace of God I am what I am: and his grace which was bestowed upon me was not in vain" (1 Cor 15:10).

14.4.6.en: Fourth: to the extent that the roots strike into the soil to bear "the life of Christ" in it, its visible branches spread out to bear the fruits of the Holy Spirit in abundance, so that it knows no barrenness or fruitlessness.

14.4.7.en: Fifth: "and his beauty shall be as the olive tree." Thus the believer bears the traits of the Lord and His life through the roots, and the fruits on the branches (the boughs), and also the beauty of the Lord and His glory within and without. As the Lord says to His bride: "and thou wast exceeding beautiful, and thou didst prosper into a kingdom. And thy renown went forth among the heathen for thy beauty: for it was perfect through my comeliness, which I had put upon thee, saith the Lord GOD" (Ezek 16:13-14).

14.4.8.en: The true believer, while awaiting the fellowship of Christ's glory in eternity, tastes the pledge of this glory or this beauty in his inner life. As St. Macarius the Great says, what he receives afterward is nothing but an extension of the pledge he enjoyed here within himself.

14.4.9.en: Sixth: "and his smell as Lebanon." When he bears the beauty of God like a fruitful olive tree, the sweet fragrance of Christ appears in him. As the Apostle says: "and maketh manifest the savour of his knowledge by us in every place. For we are unto God a sweet savour of Christ, in them that perish" (2 Cor 2:14-15).

14.4.10.en: Seventh: "They that dwell under his shadow shall return; they shall revive as the corn, and grow as the vine: the remembrance thereof shall be as the wine of Lebanon." They bear a heart open with love, to gather many under their shadows, offering them spiritual food and gladdening drink, and their way of life remains a good, lasting remembrance that bears witness to their heavenly Bridegroom.

14.4.11.en: Eighth: "Ephraim shall say, What have I to do any more with idols?!" If Ephraim was the tribe that stirred up the remaining ten tribes to idolatry, it is also the tribe that repents of this deed, declaring its hatred of evil. Thus the energies of evil in man are turned into energies of building for the sake of the kingdom of the true heavenly Bridegroom.

14.5.0.en: This is a simplified picture of God's work in the life of His people, indeed in the life of each member of them until he returns to Him in repentance and surrenders his life into His hands to work in him. For God responds to our repentance and our return to Him, saying: "I have heard him, and observed him" [8]. It is as though He were watching for our return and observing everything within us, waiting for the slightest movement on our part so that He may move toward us with His love. As the Apostle says: "Draw nigh to God, and he will draw nigh to you" (Jas 4:8).

14.5.1.en: He draws near to us like an evergreen cypress tree, saying to us: "I am like a green fir tree" [8]. He shades us so that the sun of trials cannot harm us. And the Lord assures us that He is the Giver of fruit in our life: "From me is thy fruit found" [8].

14.5.2.en: Finally, the book closes with advice that He offers to all of us, that we may be wise and return to the Lord in repentance and receive its fruit: "Who is wise, and he shall understand these things? prudent, and he shall know them? for the ways of the LORD are right, and the just shall walk in them: but the hypocrites shall fall therein" [10]. By this He kindles in us the longing to understand the ways of the Lord and to walk in them with wisdom so that we do not stumble. As Father Theophilus, one of the men of the second century, says: [He who has the desire to learn learns much; therefore it is fitting for you to strive to meet with me more in hearing the living voice, that you may grasp the truth with all exactness.]
